keyVerseText: And the men of Israel turned again upon the children of Benjamin, and smote them with the edge of the sword, as well the men of every city, as the beast, and all that came to hand: also they set on fire all the cities that they came to. came to hand: Heb. was found they came: Heb. were found
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word מְתֹם (mᵉthôm) derives from the root תָּמַם (tâmam), which conveys the idea of completion, perfection, or wholeness. This root encompasses concepts of being finished, whole, or sound, both literally and figuratively. Thus, מְתֹם carries the sense of integrity or entire soundness, going beyond a simple English gloss like "soundness" to include the idea of something being fully intact or unimpaired.
usageInScripture: מְתֹם appears four times in Scripture, consistently related to the idea of wholeness or soundness. It is sometimes used in phrases indicating the absence of soundness, such as "there is no soundness" or "disease and there is no soundness," highlighting physical or moral brokenness. In Judges 20:48, it is linked to the entirety of a city or group of men, emphasizing completeness. This range shows מְתֹם as a term that can describe both the presence and absence of integrity or health.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מְתֹם as soundness or wholeness rooted in completion enriches our grasp of biblical themes of holiness and restoration. Scripture often contrasts the ideal of perfect integrity with the reality of human brokenness, as seen in phrases denying מְתֹם. For the Christian faith, this highlights the need for divine redemption to restore what is incomplete or corrupted. Christ's work can be seen as the ultimate fulfillment of the concept of מְתֹם—bringing believers into perfect soundness and wholeness before God. Thus, the word invites reflection on God's power to complete and perfect His people.
keyVerseReflection: Judges 20:48 describes the men of Israel attacking the cities of Benjamin, smiting men and beasts, and burning the cities. The use of מְתֹם here, translated as "entire city," underscores the thoroughness and completeness of the judgment executed. It conveys that the destruction was not partial but whole, emphasizing the severity of Israel's response. This totality reflects the seriousness of sin and the need for decisive action to restore covenant faithfulness.
